title: Managing the state of overwhelm
text: For many people, overwhelm is a constant state, although it does not need to be. Most people face a large number of responsibilities, such as running errands, responding to emails, keeping up with household chores and hurrying to meetings. Although this is normal in modern life, the nervous system struggles to keep up. If no conscious effort is made to relieve this kind of stress, the adrenal glands become depleted, and illness sometimes follows. Overwhelm does not depend on how much is happening in a person's life; it depends entirely on how things are managed. Overwhelm can be examined from a neurological perspective, along with ways of reducing its impact. When circumstances exceed a person's ability to cope or integrate, the nervous system enters a stress response. The incident does not need to be life-threatening for the nervous system to trigger a fight, flight or collapse response. This process is entirely subjective. The trigger can be as simple as a “perceived threat,” such as being embarrassed in public, imagining being fired for arriving late, or having a squirrel run in front of the car. Regardless of the size of the incident, the system can enter a state of overwhelm, and the brain releases all the stress hormones that accompany it. Self-awareness can help. Many people take pride in being busy, and many feel that something is wrong if they are tired, or if they feel lazy and want to lie on the couch and stare at a wall.

text: It's over. title: They came for KFC! Trump travel ban threatens rare bonds with North Koreans
text: They didn't come for reform – they came for fried chicken. When more than a dozen North Korean economic officials toured California and New York in 2011, U.S. organizers hoped the trip would inspire ideas for market reforms and business innovations. The North Koreans quickly made it clear that was NOT why they had come. They wanted U.S. investment, especially from restaurant giant Yum! Brands Inc, said Susan Shirk, a University of California at San Diego professor who helped organize the visit. “They really wanted to get KFC to North Korea,” Shirk said, referring to the fried chicken chain. Yum, she added, did not return their interest. In recent years, a handful of visits by official delegations and athletes have offered rare chances for ordinary Americans and North Koreans to come together. Now those exchanges are in jeopardy. President Donald Trump has put North Korea in a group of nations facing travel restrictions to the United States because they do not share enough information about visa applicants. The new policy lands at a time of soaring tensions between the United States and North Korea over Pyongyang's nuclear weapons and ballistic missile tests, and escalating verbal threats from the country's leader Kim Jong Un. Will it matter? The restrictions are unlikely to have a broad impact – non-diplomatic travelers from North Korea rarely top 50 a year, according to U.S. State Department data. But human rights activists fear it has severed one of the few human bonds between the isolated country and the West. “The main point in inviting these people here is to give them exposure to the U.S., and see if one can open the door a bit,” said Roberta Cohen, co-chair emeritus for the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea.

title: Edward Snowden says journalists are an endangered species in America
text: Whistleblower Edward Snowden told reporters that in the current period of mass surveillance and collusion between the mainstream media and the state, journalists are an endangered species facing extinction. “Journalists are increasingly a threatened class when we think about the right to privacy,” Snowden said. “Yes, I can give you tips on how to protect your communications, but you are going to be engaging in an arms race that you simply cannot win.” Snowden, who spoke by video feed at a German conference, urged journalists to be brave and to oppose the system by exposing privacy violations and government intrusions to the public. “You must fight this on the front pages and you must win, if you want to be able to report in the same way that you’ve been able to do in the previous centuries.” Snowden also criticized the mainstream media for failing to hold the government to account and to prompt public debate about short-sighted and secret government policy. “Policy is only short-sighted here because it is not being publicly debated. It is not being openly scrutinized outside of this audience of a few special interests.” By failing to fulfill their duties in a functioning democracy, the mainstream media have contributed to granting the government a previously unthinkable amount of power. The Clinton presidential campaign is an example. Unconstrained by the law and not scrutinized by the media, Clinton as president will exercise a dictator's authority. Snowden believes that journalists must resume criticizing those in power and prompting public debate, and that spying and hacking should be at the top of the agenda.

title: Israeli flags burned in Berlin! German minister fires back: anti-Semitism has NO place here
text: Flames in the heart of Berlin. German Justice Minister Heiko Maas declared there was no place for anti-Semitism in Germany after demonstrators enraged by U.S. President Donald Trump's decision to recognize Jerusalem as the capital of Israel set Israeli flags alight in the German capital. On Sunday, about 2,500 people marched in Berlin against Trump's decision and one Israeli flag was burned, police said, adding that investigations into 11 people had been launched, one of them over the flag burning. And that wasn't the first time. On Friday, hundreds massed outside the U.S. embassy for “Day of Rage” protests. Police later said on Twitter they had detained 10 people and that 12 criminal charges had been brought – including for burning Israeli flags. Maas didn't hold back, telling Bild newspaper's Monday edition: “Any kind of anti-Semitism is an attack on everyone. Anti-Semitism must never be allowed to have a place (in society) again.” In Germany, anti-Semitism remains an extremely sensitive issue more than 70 years after the end of the Nazi-era Holocaust, in which 6 million Jews were killed. Germany sees itself as one of Israel's closest allies. German Foreign Minister Sigmar Gabriel told Bild that while criticism of Trump's decision was understandable, people had no right or reason to burn the Israeli flag, stir up hatred against Jews or question Israel's right to exist. Anyone who did that, he said, was taking a stand not only against Israel but against the German constitution – and Germany would not tolerate it. Gabriel said Germany only permitted peaceful demonstrations and would not let conflicts in which people were prepared to use violence be brought to Germany from other countries.

title: Spy nests on the beach? Obama slams the door on two Russian compounds!
text: For decades they were playgrounds. A pair of luxurious waterfront compounds outside New York and Washington served Russian diplomats as a retreat – places to frolic in the water, play tennis and soak in lengthy steam baths. Then came Thursday. Obama administration officials painted a very different picture: beachside spy nests, sometimes used by Russian intelligence operatives for long conversations on the sand to dodge American electronic surveillance. The order was blunt. All Russians out of the compounds within 24 hours! It was just one of a string of retaliatory measures the White House unleashed in response to what it called a Russian campaign to wreak havoc on the presidential election, and what it said was systemic harassment of American officials in Russia. And there was more. On top of shuttering the two compounds, administration officials announced the expulsion by Sunday of 35 unnamed Russian officials – and their families – who they said were working undercover as spies. Sound familiar? The announcement echoed the reprisals that were routine during the Cold War, and within hours the government of Vladimir V. Putin vowed a swift response. That all but guaranteed that the Obama administration’s final days would be swallowed up by escalating accusations and retaliation between Washington and Moscow. Yet the Obama administration offered no proof on Thursday linking the two compounds or the expelled Russians to intelligence activities, and veterans of the spy games were split on the administration’s actions. “I think these sanctions are pretty weak. It’s more perhaps symbolic,” said Steven Hall, a former senior C.I.A. official who ran Russia operations until his retirement in 2015. But Mr. Hall said the other measures could cause more irritation in Moscow.

title: House votes to ban sale and display of Confederate flag in federal cemeteries
text: The measure raises questions about the position of Southern leaders. Confederate flags should be placed on the graves of Civil War soldiers. The measure goes too far and is a hasty reaction to the shooting in Charleston, SC. The House has voted to ban the display of Confederate flags at historic federal cemeteries in the Deep South. The low-profile vote took place late Tuesday after a brief debate on a measure funding the National Park Service, which maintains 14 national cemeteries, most of which contain graves of Civil War soldiers. The proposal by California Democrat Jared Huffman would prevent the Park Service from allowing private groups to decorate the graves of southern soldiers with Confederate flags in states that commemorate Confederate Memorial Day. The cemeteries affected are the Andersonville and Vicksburg cemeteries in Georgia and Mississippi. Pressure to ban display of the flag on state and federal property has increased since last month’s murders at a historic black church in Charleston, South Carolina. The sale of Confederate flags was also banned. The House voted to affirm that stores on federal lands operated by the National Park Service cannot sell Confederate flags, in line with a new policy announced after the shooting in Charleston, S.C. The amendment to the 2016 Interior Department appropriations bill was adopted on a voice vote after six minutes of debate, during which no one spoke in opposition. The amendment reflects a policy announced by the National Park Service in June to ban the sale of Confederate flag merchandise from its gift shops and bookstores. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the author of the amendment, said it was important that Congress prevent the sale of the Confederate image on federal property.

title: House votes to ban sale and display of Confederate flags in federal cemeteries
text: The House voted late Tuesday to ban the display of Confederate flags at historic federal cemeteries in the Deep South and affirmed that stores on federal lands operated by the National Park Service cannot sell Confederate flags. The low-profile vote followed a brief debate on a measure funding the National Park Service, which maintains 14 national cemeteries, most of which contain graves of Civil War soldiers. The proposal by California Democrat Jared Huffman would bar the Park Service from allowing private groups to decorate the graves of southern soldiers with Confederate flags in states that commemorate Confederate Memorial Day. The affected cemeteries are the Andersonville and Vicksburg cemeteries in Georgia and Mississippi. Pressure to ban display of the flag on state and federal property increased after last month’s murders at a historic black church in Charleston, South Carolina. The amendment to the 2016 Interior Department appropriations bill was adopted on a voice vote after six minutes of debate. No one spoke in opposition. It reflected a policy announced by the National Park Service in June, after the shooting in Charleston, S.C., to ban the sale of Confederate flag merchandise from its gift shops and bookstores. Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), the amendment’s author, said it was important that Congress prevent the sale of the Confederate image on federal property. The measure raises questions about the position of Southern leaders. Confederate flags should be placed on the graves of Civil War soldiers. The measure went too far and was a hasty reaction to the Charleston, SC, shooting.

title: Punishing the poor: Trump's brutal budget taps working-class resentment!
text: The gasps were audible on both sides of the ideological divide. Late last month President Trump unveiled the outline of his first budget – and it proposed to slash a whopping $54 billion from the discretionary civilian budget next year to pay for a defense. That part of the budget pays for nearly everything the government does other than the military, pensions and health insurance for older people. And it has already been cut again and again. It adds up to only some $500 billion – hardly the place to balance a $4 trillion federal budget! After Mr. Trump’s proposed cuts it would be 25 percent smaller than it was in 2010, adjusted for inflation. Even Republicans in Congress, no friends of government spending, said the math made little sense. They share Mr. Trump’s twin goals of balancing the budget and slashing taxes – but they would rather square the circle by cutting the entitlements of Social Security and Medicare. So why do it? Because Mr. Trump’s approach has a powerful political logic. The frazzled, anxious men and women who voted for him like Social Security, Medicare and defense. Other government spending? Not so much. And here's the harsh truth: going after programs for the poor costs Mr. Trump little politically – it may even help him. These programs appeal to two constituencies voters show little affinity for: the poor, and urban liberal elites who can express enormous sympathy for the disenfranchised while ignoring the struggle of the white working class. Mr. Trump is not the first Republican to propose cutting programs to pay for tax cuts. But his bluntness breaks, at least rhetorically, with a Republican establishment that insists it cares about poverty.

title: Revolt brewing! Two GOP senators threaten to derail Trump's tax bill
text: Trouble in the Senate! A Republican tax bill strongly backed by President Donald Trump ran into a potential revolt on Monday from two Republican lawmakers who could stop the sweeping legislation from ever reaching the Senate floor. Senators Ron Johnson and Bob Corker, both members of the Senate Budget Committee, warned they could vote against the tax package at a Tuesday hearing – the very hearing Republican leaders hoped would send the legislation to a full Senate vote as early as Thursday. And they don't even want the same thing. Each senator is demanding different changes. Their opposition could create the first major hurdle for the Republican tax overhaul in the Senate – the same chamber where political infighting killed the party’s effort to overturn the Obamacare healthcare law earlier this year. Remember that? Corker, a prominent deficit hawk, wants his fellow Republicans to add a backstop measure to stop tax cuts from ballooning the deficit. Johnson wants a bigger tax break for “pass-through” businesses, which include small mom-and-pop enterprises as well as some large, non-corporate businesses. “If we develop a fix prior to committee, I’ll probably support it, but if we don’t, I’ll vote against it,” Johnson’s office quoted him telling reporters in his home state of Wisconsin. The margin is razor-thin: Republicans have only a one-vote majority on the 23-member budget committee. The potential “no” votes surfaced after Congress’ Joint Committee on Taxation (JCT) estimated the Republican bill would swell the $20 trillion national debt by a staggering $1.4 trillion over a decade. Republicans insist that economic growth spurred by tax cuts would generate enough new tax revenue to wipe out any new deficit. But Corker said JCT is not expected to release a full macroeconomic analysis of the tax bill before a Senate vote, making a safeguard provision necessary. “I’m not threatening anything.”

title: No team, no plan: Trump's tax reform promise is in trouble!
text: Where is the plan? President Donald Trump has neither a clear White House tax plan nor enough staff to push through a planned tax reform, according to interviews with people in the administration, in Congress and among U.S. tax experts. Sound familiar? Just like its attempt to roll back Obamacare – which ended in an embarrassing collapse in Congress – the Trump administration has vowed quick action on taxes. Yet it still has not appointed people with the skills to evaluate complex tax laws, draft legislation and sell it to deeply divided lawmakers. Stung by last week’s failed healthcare measure, largely written by House of Representatives Republicans, Trump is determined not to lean on Congress so heavily this time for the details on taxes, his second major legislative initiative. But that only makes his lack of a strong White House tax team more glaring. Many policy options are still on the table, from deficit-funded tax cuts to a European-style value-added tax. “They’re still sorting out who’s in charge, who’s going to take the lead,” said William Hoagland, a longtime Senate Republican aide who worked on the last successful comprehensive tax reform effort in 1986. “You need someone who has the ear and support of the president who can sell a tax plan, and you need the technical support for that person,” said Hoagland, now senior vice president at the Bipartisan Policy Center, a think tank. And the markets are noticing. Financial markets have been reassessing expectations of fast action on taxes – expectations that helped fuel a Trump stocks rally. Members of Trump’s tax team are known, but not their exact duties. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin and National Economic Council Director Gary Cohn are senior team leaders.

title: How to build a bee hotel to support bee populations
text: Building a bee hotel is easier and more enjoyable than it appears. While honeybees, which live together in a self-made hive, are widely known and discussed, there is less concern about the bee species that are native to North America and are easier to help. Many other species, such as mason bees and leafcutter bees, are critical to pollination and are suffering from habitat loss. Because these bees are solitary, their presence is not overwhelming, and the hotels can be built in a backyard without the risk of attracting hundreds of bees at a time. Native bees require much less to be comfortable, according to Becky Griffin, community and school garden coordinator at the Center for Urban Agriculture and University of Georgia Extension for the Northwest District of Georgia. “Native bees nest in hollow logs, dead trees and in the ground, and when the forest is clean cut, the native bees have fewer and fewer places to nest.” Griffin said. As the spaces available for nesting decrease, so does the population of bees needed to keep the continent’s plants pollinated and healthy. Building a nesting site contributes to the health of the population and, according to Griffin, is also very rewarding. “Once you start noticing native bees, attracting them and learning about them, you’ll just want to sit on your bench in your garden and watch them work,” Griffin said. “They are amazing creatures!” A guide to building the hotel follows, with advice from Griffin and answers to frequently asked questions. Basic hotel design: the essential part of building the hotel is having the right design.

title: Trump asks O’Reilly ‘Do you think our country is so innocent?’ after host calls Putin ‘a killer’
text: Regardless of views on Donald Trump, many people would likely acknowledge that it is notable to see a US President say that the US is not as innocent as some commentators and consumers of mainstream news may believe. In an interview aired before the Super Bowl, FOX News host Bill O’Reilly questioned President Trump’s comments about working with Russia in the fight against ISIS. In doing so, O’Reilly called Putin a killer. Trump responded: “There are a lot of killers. We’ve got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country is so innocent?” Further details of the interview follow. O’Reilly, apparently surprised, asked him why. “He is the leader of his country. I say it’s better to get along with Russia than not, and if Russia helps us in the fight against ISIS which is a major fight and the Islamic terrorism all over the world, that’s a good thing,” Trump answered. “Will I get along with him? I have no idea.” O’Reilly then challenged Trump, calling the Russian president a killer. Trump dismissed the comment, saying: “There are a lot of killers. We’ve got a lot of killers. What, do you think our country is so innocent?” It is not the first time Trump has made such comments when journalists have questioned his position on the Russian leader. At the end of 2015, the host of MSNBC’s Morning Joe told Trump that Putin kills journalists. The then-presidential candidate replied: “I think that our country does plenty of killing, too, Joe. I’ve always felt fine about Putin. He’s a strong leader.”

title: U.S. News and World Report publishes list of the 10 most popular countries for refugees
text: More than 21,000 people from all regions of the world took part in the Best Countries survey, in which they assessed how closely they associated 80 countries with specific characteristics. Four of these characteristics, economically stable, good job market, income equality and is a place I would live, were included in the Best Countries to Be an Immigrant ranking. Countries were also scored relative to others on the share of migrants in their population and on the amount of remittances the migrants they host sent home. They were also graded on a United Nations assessment of the integration measures provided for immigrants, such as language training and transfers of job certifications, and on the rationale behind current integration policies. The editor noted that the measures concern integration, not assimilation. Ann Corcoran of Refugee Resettlement Watch wrote that remittances are important because they are money sent out of the host economy, and that economic studies seeking to show the benefits of migration to a country never account for how much of migrants’ earnings or welfare payments are sent out of the country and lost to the host economy. The ranking is as follows: 1. Sweden, which Corcoran has long ranked as the country most likely to fall to Islamists; 2. Canada, where the northern border should be fortified; 3. Switzerland; 4. Australia; 5. Germany; 6. Norway; 7. US; 8. Netherlands; 9. Finland; 10. Denmark. Arab, mostly Muslim, countries are not among the desired destinations.

title: Chaos in Chicago! Trump rally scrapped as rival crowds clash
text: It all fell apart. U.S. presidential candidate Donald Trump canceled a rally scheduled for Friday night in Chicago after the event descended into a chaotic scene, with thousands of attendees split into opposing camps of supporters of the Republican front-runner and protesters inflamed by his candidacy. Nearly a half hour after the rally was supposed to start, a Trump campaign staffer took the stage and announced it would be postponed for safety reasons. A campaign statement issued shortly after said the event would be held on another, unspecified day. Then the crowd erupted in chants and cheers. Scuffles broke out as signs were ripped from hands, and police moved in fast to defuse the most serious clashes. Cries of “We dumped Trump! We dumped Trump!” rang out inside the University of Illinois at Chicago pavilion where the event was held. A rival group shot back: “We want Trump! We want Trump!” Outside, chants of “We shut it down!” rippled through the crowd as news of the cancellation spread. And it was no accident. Chicago activists had spent the whole week before the rally planning how to disrupt it. Trump has become an intensely polarizing candidate in the presidential campaign. He has inspired impassioned supporters and ignited a furious backlash with his promise to build a wall along the U.S.-Mexican border to keep out illegal immigrants and his call to temporarily ban the entry of Muslims into the country. One group at Friday’s event, Showing Up for Racial Justice, coordinated with minority student groups on campuses, using group email chains and messaging so protesters could stay in constant communication. Did they expect to win? One of the organizers, Nathaniel Lewis, 25, a master’s degree student in public health at the University of Illinois at Chicago, said he was shocked they succeeded in shutting the rally down.

title: Virginia cracks down! First state to tame the fantasy sports frenzy
text: Virginia just made history. Governor Terry McAuliffe has signed a bill making the state the first in the United States to regulate fantasy sports – a multibillion-dollar online business whose legality has been challenged across the country. The rules are tough. The measure signed by McAuliffe, a Democrat, requires players to be 18 or older, offers players limits on how much they can bet, demands annual audits and bars employees from competing in company contests. It takes effect on July 1. “This bill, which was passed by super majorities of both chambers, will empower Virginia to regulate this emerging industry and keep consumers safe from abuses,” Brian Coy, a McAuliffe spokesman, said in a statement. The governor signed the bill on Monday. Why now? The booming fantasy sports industry, dominated by DraftKings and FanDuel, has come under growing scrutiny from state regulators over the past year, with the attorneys general of New York, Illinois and Nevada questioning their legality. The games are illegal in several states. The companies charge customers to play mostly single-day games in which they draft a roster of players whose performance on the field earns points. And the industry giants? In statements on a sports gaming website, spokesmen for DraftKings and FanDuel welcomed the Virginia measure. Meanwhile, Texas struck a deal with FanDuel last week under which the company will halt paid operations in the state on May 2!

title: McMullin responds after Trump calls him a puppet
text: Evan McMullin responded on Twitter after Republican nominee Donald Trump on Saturday called him “a puppet of a loser” whom no one has heard of. “Yes you’ve never heard of me because while you were harassing women at beauty pageants, I was fighting terrorists abroad.” McMullin wrote. The tweet received more than 6,000 likes in under an hour. McMullin has performed strongly in Utah, finishing ahead of both Trump and Hillary Clinton in one poll, although some suggest what they call the Mormon Mafia was responsible for his rise. The momentum drew Trump's attention. Twitter users noted that Trump and Pence had begun to criticize McMullin and that Trump had called him Bill Kristol's puppet, apparently his first comment about McMullin after choosing to ignore him. Others highlighted Trump's claim that McMullin was "going from coffee shop to coffee shop" to win Utah, with one user telling McMullin that Trump was jealous of his effective coffee shop campaign in Utah. The Mormon community has driven coffee almost entirely out of the state, though residents remain engaged in the election. The number of likes indicated that some people know who McMullin is. Rick Wilson congratulated McMullin on Twitter, writing that a candidate has made an impact when Trump starts insulting him.

title: Free for all! The New York Times throws open its doors for the election
text: The paywall is coming down! The New York Times is inviting readers to dive into its reporting, analysis and commentary from the run-up through the aftermath of the 2016 election. For 72 hours, readers get unlimited access to NYTimes.com – from 12:01 a.m. ET on Monday, November 7 until 11:59 p.m. ET on Wednesday, November 9. “This is an important moment for our country,” said Arthur Sulzberger, Jr., publisher of The New York Times. “Independent journalism is crucial to democracy and I believe there is no better time to show readers the type of original journalism The New York Times creates every day.” So what's on offer for this historic election? Plenty. Follow The Times’s live coverage on election night, with reporting on hundreds of races across the country and analysis by the political team. The Upshot plans to deliver live forecasts of the Presidential and Senate elections, just as it did during the 2016 primaries and the 2014 Senate midterms. These forecasts give readers a constantly updated estimate of the final vote, based on turnout patterns, exit polling and the demographics of places where votes have already been counted. The New York Times mobile news apps are free to download. Users can sign up for breaking news notifications to stay on top of major news events. Readers can also sign up for free newsletters and get more of The New York Times delivered straight to their inbox. And there's more: a livestream of election coverage on The Times’s Facebook page, running all night from 4:30 p.m. ET. Expect live video reports from correspondents at polling stations across the country, as well as college campuses, election viewing parties and more!

title: Trump’s use of the word ‘bigly’ is explained
text: During the election campaign, a great deal has become known about Republican candidate Donald Trump. One aspect of his speech, however, has puzzled many people: his use of the word ‘bigly.’ Its meaning has been unclear, including whether he uses it in the way that words such as ‘largely’ or ‘finally’ are used, whether its opposite would be ‘littlely’, and whether it reflects a poor command of English. He has used the word frequently in campaign speeches, and it has at times been transcribed and reported as ‘bigly.’ Some people concluded that he is actually saying ‘big league.’ Others were not certain. The issue turns out to be one of pronunciation rather than vocabulary. Raymond Navarro of Catholic broadcaster EWTN asked Trump directly in an interview this week whether he was saying ‘bigly’ or ‘big league.’ Trump responded: “I use big league.” The exchange appears at 25:05 in a video clip of the interview. That he says ‘big league’ was also confirmed by his son Donald Trump Jr., who was asked about it after the September 26 presidential debate. The question has therefore been settled. Before it was, broadcast and social media made extensive humorous use of the word. A clip from Bloomberg, made before the answer was known, illustrates the confusion over ‘bigly’ and ‘big league.’
